intro: Thirteen centuries ago, an Umayyad caliph raised an octagon of stone and a dome of gold over Jerusalem's holiest rock. This is the story of the oldest great monument of Islamic architecture.
page_title: Dome of the Rock: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: Completed in 691-692 CE under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik, the Dome of the Rock is among the oldest surviving monuments of Islamic architecture. Its plan is pure geometry: a central dome about 20 m in diameter on an elevated circular drum carried by 4 piers and 12 columns, ringed by an octagonal arcade of 24 piers and columns, all enclosed by octagonal outer walls with sides of about 18 m. Four entrances face the cardinal directions. The dome is a double shell: an inner wooden dome beneath the gilded outer one.
sections.heading: Geometry in stone

sections.body: The shrine encloses the Foundation Stone, about 13 by 7.6 m, sacred to all three Abrahamic faiths: in Jewish tradition the site of the Temple, in Christian tradition tied to Jesus's final days, in Islamic tradition the rock of Muhammad's Night Journey. The building's inscriptions, among the earliest extensive Quranic texts in architecture, proclaim the new faith in the idiom of Byzantine mosaic. In the 16th century the Ottomans faced the exterior in the blue tiles seen today.
sections.heading: The rock at the center

sections.body:
The Dome of the Rock has no Hollywood career, and that is the point. Unlike Hagia Sophia it is almost never a film location: its sanctity and the politics of the Temple Mount keep fiction crews away. Instead it has become something rarer, the most reproduced sacred skyline on earth. It is Jerusalem's visual shorthand: the golden dome that means the city in news broadcasts, magazine covers, and documentaries worldwide, from Willy Lindwer's The Temple Mount Is Mine (2003) to the IMAX film Jerusalem (2013), which tours the Old City's holy places in giant-screen detail.

The building's image does political work too. Its likeness anchors debates over heritage and sovereignty, reproduced on everything from textbooks to protest banners. Thirteen centuries after Abd al-Malik raised it, the dome still does what it was built to do: proclaim, in gold visible from every approach to the city, that this rock and this skyline matter.
